TRW-Gifts IT2-VP — what’s running and why it converts

Aug 3 – Sep 1 2026 (30 days) · Meta · source: ejam-dwh cro_dashboard_ads (page-level funnel, every step measured the same way on every page) · ads with $900+ spend · rebuilt Sep 2

ROAS = Meta-attributed in-platform revenue ÷ spend. Comparable across creatives, not a P&L number.

Contribution = revenue + upsell revenue − cost of goods − merchant fees − ad spend, the Goal Pacing dashboard’s Contribution (agency fees are not allocated in this table). CM % = Contribution ÷ revenue, the dashboard’s Contr. Margin %. Negative means the first order lost money; nine in ten orders here are subscriptions, so rebills are the payback.

Every creative below is clickable. Videos play in a new tab, statics open full size, and each card links to the live Facebook post.

One correction before the call

IT2-VP is our highest-spend page, not our highest-converting one. Same 30 days, same channel, funnel table rather than the creative dashboard, so every step below is measured identically on every page.

IT2-VP wins the auction and loses the page. It converts LP views to orders 36% worse than the FrontrowMD build living under the original TRW-Gifts URL, at a $8 higher CPA, and it needed 58% more LP views to produce roughly the same order count (1,939 vs 1,228 on the ads this report covers).

The entire gap sits at one step: LP view → add to cart, 19.0% vs 34.3%. Add-to-cart here is the click from the page into checkout, and checkout views confirm it within 3% on every page, so this is not an event-timing artifact. Once someone is in checkout, all four pages behave the same: 6% enter payment details, 8 to 10% order. The checkout does not care which page fed it. The ads do, and that is section 3.

On contribution margin the order is the same, the level is lower. No page here pays for itself on the first order. IT2-VP’s contribution for the month is −$78k on $158k of attributed revenue, a −49% contribution margin. The FrontrowMD build sits at −$56k and −34%, the Holiday control at −$10k and −20%. Per order that is $38, $27 and $17 given back. Nine in ten orders on all of these pages are subscriptions, so each page pays back on rebills, and the smaller the first-order hole, the fewer rebills it takes. Judged on the money, the gap between IT2-VP and its sibling is not eight dollars of CPA. It is $22k more lost in the month for the same number of orders.

Two things the table hides. First, “the original TRW-Gifts page” is three different page builds behind one URL, and the two that convert at 34 to 37% are what IT2-VP should be tested against. Second, IT2-VP and the FrontrowMD build are the same template (same banner, same “10 Reasons” structure, same comparison table, same offer block) with a different headline and a different first two reasons, and they have never run the same ad: 92 creatives on IT2-VP, 24 on FrontrowMD, zero shared. The page comparison is fully confounded with creative. Click any page name to open it.

Clean read: hold the creative set constant and split IT2-VP against the FrontrowMD build on the same five ads. That test has never been run, so nobody actually knows which page is better. What we do know is what the traffic does, and that is section 3.

3. Why the creative is working

One variable underneath, the price of the click, and six mechanisms that decide it. Each mechanism is called out in a purple box in the section it belongs to.

1. The closed loop Curiosity opens a loop, the click closes it, and a closed loop has nothing left when the price appears at checkout.Ref: SH-16478-7▶ vs SH-17273-9↗
2. Re-orientation cost Any promise the page fails to confirm makes the visitor stop and work out where they are.Ref: SH-16313-2↗ vs SH-16192▶
3. Deliberation carries A question asked in the ad is still being answered at the cart.Ref: SH-16535-9↗ vs SH-16464-8↗
4. The ad as the page When the ad borrows the page’s layout, orientation cost is zero and add-to-cart fires immediately.Ref: SH-16313-2↗ vs SH-16674-7↗
5. Division of labour The ad transfers desire, the page makes the argument. An ad that argues leaves the page nothing to do.Ref: SH-16478-7▶ vs SH-17207-4▶
6. Anchor before arrival A price named in the ad turns the page’s offer into confirmation instead of negotiation.Ref: SH-16521-10↗ vs SH-16158↗

3.1 The price of the click sets the funnel

Every ad on this page can be priced by what one landing-page view costs (spend divided by LP views). That single number predicts the whole funnel: correlation with add-to-cart +0.66, with checkout close +0.76, with payment-entry +0.63. Cheap visitors fail at the page and at the payment form.

Thirteen cheap-click ads bring 65% of the visitors these 62 ads send to the page, at 14.6% add-to-cart. The premium third brings 12% of visitors at 32.1%. Blend them and you get the page’s 19%. The page did not get worse; the mix did.

The cleanest proof is one creative at two prices. SH-17250-3↗ and SH-17250-10↗ are the same static, same headline, same bag, same bullets, same “$2.69 per bag” line, with a slightly different layout. Meta priced them differently: $40 CPM against $24, $3.77 against $0.60 per LP view. Same artwork, and the cheap version converts at 14.8% add-to-cart and closes 7.5%, against 34.3% and 16.8% for the expensive one. Nothing about the ad changed. The buyer did.

In June the page ran 49% add-to-cart at $2.64 a view, and the launch statics (“Can’t pick a favorite? Now you don’t have to,” “Two new variety packs just dropped”) returned 1.6 to 2.1 ROAS at $37 to $46 CPA. Two things happened after: audience broadening in July took ATC from 49% to 27% at a flat $3.30 a view, then the cheap-click creative arrived (the couch video Jul 30, the macro statics Aug 4) and halved the click price while ATC fell to 18%. The page can convert at 40 to 60%. It has been doing so all along for the visitors who cost enough to want it.

Margin follows the same line. The premium third runs a −22% contribution margin (−$10k on $47k of revenue); the cheap third runs −60% (−$27k on $45k). Same CPA, three times the loss per revenue dollar: cheap clicks are not cheaper orders, they are the same price with a smaller basket behind them.

What this means for the call: judge the page on the premium cohort, judge creative on contribution margin, CPA and LP-view-to-order, and never on blended add-to-cart. And read every mechanism below as a description of which ads buy expensive visitors and which buy cheap ones.

3.2 The two lists barely overlap, and that is the finding

Rank by spend and rank by ROAS and you get almost entirely different ads. Meta is buying attention. Attention is not intent.

This is not a story about a handful of ads. Across all 62 creatives on this page with more than $900 of spend, click-through rate runs inverse to add-to-cart rate (correlation −0.50), inverse to ROAS (−0.37), and most strongly of all inverse to the checkout close (−0.65). The harder an ad works to win the click, the less likely that click buys, and the place it fails hardest is the payment page.

Checkout close explains ROAS on this page (correlation 0.72) far better than add-to-cart does (0.46). The high-click third gets people to checkout, where they see the price and leave: 3.8% of their checkout visitors enter payment details, against 11.8% for the quiet-clicking third.

MechanismThe closed loop

Curiosity and negation headlines (“We can’t say what those 22g of protein are doing to your stomach”, “Our lawyers made us cross this out”, “Amazon’s record-breaking candy”) open a loop. The click closes it. A closed loop has no purchase drive left in it, so the page has to start the sale from zero, and the moment the price appears there is nothing underneath it. That is why these ads lose most at checkout, not at the page: their visitors add to cart out of momentum and stop at the payment form. Product-and-offer-forward creative pre-sells the actual thing, so the price reads as expected.

Proves it
SH-16478-7▶8s pineapple. No claim, so no loop to close.0.71% CTR → 12.2% pay info · 1.75
SH-16521-10↗Offer stated up front, price arrives expected.0.94% CTR → 16.7% pay info · 1.64
Breaks it
SH-17273-9↗Record-breaking candy. Loop shuts on the click, $34k behind it.3.56% CTR → 5.4% pay info · 0.72
SH-17272-5↗Protein-bar wedge, same shape.3.87% CTR → 5.0% pay info · 0.93

Implication for CRO: a large share of what looks like page underperformance is the page absorbing curiosity traffic it was never written to convert. And the fix for that traffic sits partly on the checkout, not the LP: the price needs its anchor (the strike-through, the “up to 46% off” ladder, the free gifts) visible before the total, because these visitors arrive without one.

3.3 Message match is doing more work than any page element

Page headline: “10 Reasons To Try Our 5 NEW Gummy Flavors Before Any Other Candy In 2026”. It is a flavor-novelty page. Ads that promise flavor novelty convert on it. Ads that promise something else do not.

Ad promiseLP→ATC
“All our best flavors. One bag.”44.1%
POV side-script UGC (SH-16469▶)47.7%
“This month’s Shameless box”41.9%
“Four new flavors you won’t find on a shelf”33.8%
Fiber-wedge / protein-bar comparison statics12–16%
MechanismRe-orientation cost

Every promise the page fails to confirm forces the visitor to re-orient before they can shop. The page does have a comparison table above the fold, but it compares against traditional candy. The wedge statics promised a fight with protein bars, so the table confirms nothing they came for. Same with price: SH-16192 promises $2.69 a bag and the page shows a discount ladder instead. The first thing those visitors do is work out where they are, and that pause is where they leave.

Proves it
SH-16147-4↗“All our best flavors. One bag.” The page says this too.44.1% ATC · 1.13
SH-16313-2↗Six badged bags, the page’s own range.41.9% ATC · 1.51
Breaks it
SH-15456↗Menopause permission line on a flavor-novelty page.8.7% ATC, lowest of 62 · 0.75
SH-16192▶Promises $2.69 a bag. The page shows a ladder instead.36.9% ATC → 10.9% close

3.4 Variety as acquisition beats variety as choice

Acquisition framing (“get all of them”): SH-16535-9 fans four packs and closes with “NEW DROP · ONLINE ONLY · GET ALL FOUR FIRST.” 1.55 ROAS, $50 CPA, 15.6% checkout close. Same family: “This month’s box” (1.51, 14.1% close), “All our best flavors. One bag.” (1.13).

Choice framing (“pick one”): “Berry lover, or tropical soul?”, “All the all-stars, or all the berries?” These pull respectable ATC (35.7%, 33.1%) and then close at 8.7% and 8.2%, roughly half the acquisition group, with only 2 to 3% of checkout visitors entering payment details. ROAS 1.01 and 1.01.

MechanismDeliberation carries

A question asked in the ad is still being answered at the cart. The choice framing pulls respectable add-to-cart and then loses half of it at checkout, because someone asked to pick arrives still picking. Acquisition framing removes the decision entirely: the unit of purchase becomes the set. For a page whose core product is the variety pack, the frame is “you don’t have to pick.”

Proves it
SH-16535-9↗“Get all four.” The set is the unit, no decision left.33.8% ATC → 15.6% close · 1.55
SH-16313-2↗Six bags, one box. Nothing left to pick.41.9% ATC → 14.1% close · 1.51
Breaks it
SH-16464-8↗“Berry lover, or tropical soul?” Asks the visitor to pick.35.7% ATC → 8.7% close · 1.01
SH-16461-17↗“All the all-stars, or all the berries?”33.1% ATC → 8.2% close · 1.01

3.5 The best static is a menu, and that is the finding for the page

SH-16313-2 has the highest LP→ATC of any static on the page: 41.9%, double the page average, at 1.51 ROAS.

It is not a hook. It is a menu. Six bags in a grid, each with a badge (#1 NEW DROP, TROPICAL FAV, FAN FAVORITE, SOUR PICK, CULT CLASSIC, BEST SELLER) and a one-line flavor description. Then a proof row (70 cal, 3g sugar, 26g fiber) and a risk-reversal line, “Cancel anytime.”

That is the landing page’s own listicle structure compressed into one square. The visitor arrives already oriented: they know the range, social proof is attached to specific bags, and they have picked a favorite before the page loads. Re-orientation cost is zero, so ATC fires fast.

MechanismThe ad as the page

When the ad borrows the page’s layout, not just its words, re-orientation cost drops to zero and add-to-cart fires immediately. The visitor already knows the range, already has social proof attached to specific bags, and has already picked a favourite before the page loads.

Proves it
SH-16313-2↗The listicle layout compressed into one square.41.9% ATC, best static · 1.51
SH-16158↗“Two new variety packs just dropped.” Same product, same words.32.5% ATC · 1.00
Breaks it
SH-16674-7↗Strong static, nothing on the page confirms it.13.3% ATC · $109 CPA
SH-17273-9↗Macro photo, three claims, no layout the page repeats.15.9% ATC on $34,412

If the call takes one thing from this report: the highest-ATC ad is the one that looks most like the page. Message match is not a copy exercise, it is a layout exercise. The badge system is doing the ranking work the “10 reasons” headline promises but the grid does not currently deliver.

3.6 Short product motion beats long creator storytelling here

Format first: the typical video on this page beats the typical static, 1.13 median ROAS against 0.85, and a median checkout close of 12.6% against 8.8%. On dollars the two formats tie, because 41% of all video spend sits in the one video that performs worst. Then, within video, length and frame decide the rest.

CreativeLengthROASCPAHook rateWatch
SH-16478-7▶8s1.75$4414.6%Play
SH-16468-6▶17s1.20$6516.6%Play
SH-16481-5▶24s0.77$9921.5%Play
SH-17207-4▶42s0.54$11738.2%Play

The two extremes matter more than the runtime. SH-16478-7▶, the best ad on the page, is a single pineapple gummy on flat bright blue with one word on it: PINEAPPLE. No claim, no fiber number, no offer, no person. Pure appetite. 1.75 ROAS at half the page CPA.

SH-17207-4, the biggest spender, is two women on a couch turning a bag over to read the nutrition panel, captioned “So, this is a new one.” It hooks at 38.2% because label-inspection is native and human. But it is a scrutiny frame, not a desire frame. Nobody in it is eating. It recruits people in evaluation mode and sends them to a page written for people in wanting mode. That is the 0.54 in one sentence. Its visitors reach checkout and only 3.7% enter payment details.

MechanismDivision of labour

The ad’s job is to transfer desire. The page’s job is to make the argument. An ad that makes the argument itself leaves the page nothing to do but repeat it, and repetition reads as a stall. Eight seconds of product in motion spends no argument at all, which is why the page can close behind it.

Proves it
SH-16478-7▶8s of product motion. Spends no argument at all.1.75 · $44 CPA
SH-16468-6▶17s overheard POV. Sets up, never closes.29.8% ATC → 18.5% close · 1.20
Breaks it
SH-17207-4▶42s of nutrition-panel scrutiny. Argument finished in feed.0.54 · $117 CPA
SH-16481-5▶24s of rotation, blank poster frame, no escalation.21.5% hook → 13.6% hold · 0.77

3.7 Stating the offer in the ad anchors the page

SH-16521-10 is literally “GET UP TO 46% OFF + FREE GIFTS” and returns 1.64 ROAS at $58 CPA. The page’s own offer, said out loud before the click. It has the best payment-entry rate on the page, 16.7% of checkout visitors, three times the high-click ads. As of Sep 2 the page carries a Labor Day banner with the same offer in the hero; keep an offer line there after the sale ends.

MechanismAnchor before arrival

A price stated in the ad becomes the reference point the visitor carries onto the page, so the discount ladder reads as confirmation rather than negotiation. Ads that stay silent on price make the page introduce it cold, and a cold price gets compared to the supermarket shelf instead of to our own anchor.

Proves it
SH-16521-10↗“GET UP TO 46% OFF + FREE GIFTS.” Price named pre-click.16.7% pay info → 17.9% close · 1.64
SH-17250-3↗Resolves onto product facts and $2.69. Nothing left to surprise.16.2% pay info → 16.8% close · 1.31
Breaks it
SH-16158↗Builds real desire, names no price. Checkout introduces it cold.32.5% ATC → 12.4% close · 1.00
SH-16481-5▶Product motion, no offer, no anchor.29.9% ATC → 5.8% pay info · 0.77

4. What I would take to the call

  • Bring contribution margin into the room. The page’s contribution for the month is −$78k, a −49% contribution margin on first orders, and nine in ten orders are subscriptions, so rebills are the payback clock. Only five of 62 ads are contribution-positive, all capped near $1,450. Rank the page and its creative on contribution margin and rebills-to-payback, not on ROAS.
  • Stop calling IT2-VP the top converter. It is the top spender. The FrontrowMD build under the original TRW-Gifts URL converts LP views 57% better at an $8 lower CPA, and the event map is confirmed identical.
  • The checkout is where high-click traffic dies: 3.8% payment entry versus 11.8%. Every page closes checkout the same, so this is an anchoring problem, not a page problem. Put the strike-through and the “up to 46% off + free gifts” line above the total on the checkout, and keep an offer line in the LP hero after the Labor Day banner comes down.
  • SH-17273-9 is a quarter of page spend at 0.72 ROAS and a −67% contribution margin (−$18k for the month), with a 5.4% payment-entry rate. Rewrite the overlay or cap it. The rest of the page runs 0.86 ROAS and −39% margin without it, against −45% with it.
  • Report add-to-cart by click-price cohort from now on. IT2-VP at 19% blended is 32% on premium clicks and 15% on cheap ones, and 65% of its visitors are cheap ones. The page is being graded on traffic it was never fed before August.
  • Pull SH-17259-7↗ today. It is live at $1,027 with a production note rendered inside the image: “*40-bag subscription tier — confirm channel before use.”
  • Run the clean test: same five creatives, IT2-VP vs TRW-Gifts, split evenly. Only way to separate page from traffic.
  • On the page: lead with acquisition not choice; put “up to 46% off + 4 free gifts” in the hero; add a comparison block so comparison-ad traffic gets resolved; rebuild the flavor grid to match SH-16313-2 with a badge and a one-line description on every bag.
  • On media buying: three creatives are scaled, the rest are pinned at $1,450, and the three scaled ads are the three worst ROAS performers in the top eight. The typical video beats the typical static on every money metric, but the one video that was scaled is the worst one. SH-16478-7 at 1.75 ROAS and $44 CPA, one of the five contribution-positive ads, has never been let off the leash.
